summary: A revision of RFC 2301 describing the TIFF representation of image data used for Internet fax. It is based on feedback and on independent implementation and interoperability testing since 1998, with changes summarized in an annex.

eli5.summary: It explains how to save a fax page as a picture file in a standard way, so every fax machine and computer can open it.

subtitle: How a fax page is stored as a TIFF file, in six profiles from plain black-and-white to mixed color.

tldr.problem: Internet fax needs one agreed way to put fax page images and their settings into a file, so that fax machines, mail systems and computers can all read them.
tldr.mechanism: TIFF-FX inserts the compressed fax image data into a TIFF file and uses TIFF fields to describe it, with values that comply with the ITU-T fax recommendations. Six profiles (S, F, J, C, L, M) pick subsets of fields and compression methods.
tldr.outcome: Every implementation must support the minimal black-and-white Profile S, and color implementations must also support Profile C. This RFC revises RFC 2301 and is a Draft Standard.

today: RFC 3949 is a Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 2301. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its MIME registration is covered in RFC 3950.

sections.title: Faxes as TIFF Files
sections.content:
RFC 3949 describes how to use TIFF (Tag Image File Format) to represent the data and structure produced by the ITU-T Recommendations for Group 3 facsimile. The result is commonly known as TIFF-FX (TIFF for Fax eXtended). It is a revision of RFC 2301, based on discussion and on independent implementation and interoperability testing since March 1998.

The approach is simple: insert the compressed fax image data into a TIFF file and use TIFF fields to encode the parameters that describe it. The field values comply with the ITU-T Recommendations. TIFF's pages, images and strips let a file keep the structure of the fax data stream, and the RFC recommends a file structure that suits low-memory and page-level streaming implementations.

The RFC says references to this format should always use the term "TIFF-FX", because some profiles may not be interpreted correctly by other TIFF applications.
sections.eli5: A fax page is just a picture. This RFC says how to save that picture in a common file type, and which labels to attach so the next reader knows how to show it.

sections.title: The Six Profiles
sections.content:
A profile is a subset of the permitted TIFF fields and values for fax, tied to a group of ITU-T coding methods. There are six:

  • S: minimal black-and-white, using binary MH compression.
  • F: extended black-and-white, using MH, MR and MMR compression.
  • J: lossless JBIG black-and-white.
  • C: lossy color and grayscale, using JPEG compression.
  • L: lossless color and grayscale, using JBIG compression.
  • M: mixed raster content, combining existing compression methods.

All implementations MUST implement Profile S, and all color implementations MUST implement Profile C. An implementation of a profile MUST also implement the profiles on the path that connects it to the root of the profile tree, and MAY implement others. For example, an implementation of Profile M must also implement Profiles C and S, and may optionally implement F, J or L.
sections.eli5: Think of six kinds of crayon boxes. The smallest box, S, must be in every kit. Fancier boxes add more colors, but they always come with the smaller box they build on.

sections.title: TIFF File Structure for Fax
sections.content:
A TIFF file begins with an 8-byte header. The first two bytes give the byte order: II (0x4949, little-endian) or MM (0x4D4D, big-endian). The next two bytes hold the value 42. The last four bytes are the offset of the first image file directory (IFD). Profile S files SHALL use II.

An IFD is a sequence of tagged fields sorted by tag value: a 2-byte count, the field entries, and a 4-byte offset to the next IFD. Each field entry is 12 bytes. Each raster image in the file has its own IFD, and the image itself is stored as one or more strips of compressed data.

All fax profiles represent a multi-page document as a linked list of IFDs. Each IFD has a PageNumber field that counts from 0, and a NewSubFileType bit that marks it as one page of a multi-page document. Readers SHALL read multiple IFDs. The RFC recommends that pages be ordered in the file as in a fax data stream, and it adds an optional GlobalParametersIFD field that gathers session parameters in one place, ideally in the first IFD.

Where attributes appear both in the compressed data stream and in a TIFF field, the data stream wins for values needed to interpret the data, and the TIFF field wins for informational values such as author name.
sections.eli5: The file is like a photo album. The first page tells you how the album is arranged, and each following page has a small label and then the picture itself.

sections.title: Fields Common to All Profiles
sections.content:
Several fields are required by every profile, such as ImageWidth, ImageLength, PageNumber, RowsPerStrip, StripOffsets and StripByteCounts. Others are required with values that depend on the profile: Compression, FillOrder, PhotometricInterpretation, XResolution and YResolution, among others.

Fax data appears on the phone line in bit-reversed order relative to the ITU-T description, so most fax implementations store it with FillOrder=2 (least significant bit first). Resolutions are the ones fax allows: for example 100, 200, 300 and 400 pixels per inch, with metric equivalents. Writers SHOULD express resolution in inch-based units.

This RFC also defines new fields. FaxProfile says which profile applies to the file, and CodingMethods is a bit field saying which coding methods are in use. ProfileType, VersionYear and ModeNumber add further descriptive detail. Optional fields such as DateTime, ImageDescription, Orientation and Software are recommended for all profiles except S.
sections.eli5: Each page gets a label with its size, how sharp it is and how it was squashed. A few labels are on every page; the rest depend on which kind of fax it is.

sections.title: The Black-and-White Profiles S, F and J
sections.content:
Profile S is the minimal interchange set. It uses 1-dimensional Modified Huffman (MH) compression (Compression=3), FillOrder=2, a single page width of 1728 pixels, and a little-endian file. It has no recommended fields. Its layout is strict: one IFD per page in page order, each IFD before its image data, and each page's image data in a single strip. A 12-bit EOL sequence MUST precede each line of MH data. Writers SHOULD NOT include the RTC sequence (6 consecutive EOLs), but readers MUST handle files without RTCs and SHOULD handle files with them.

Profile F (TIFF-F) is a superset of S. It adds Modified READ (MR) and Modified Modified READ (MMR) compression, both bit orders, more page widths and more resolutions. The RFC notes that TIFF-F was never previously documented as a standard, and this document is its formal definition for Internet use. Writers seeking greater efficiency SHOULD use T.6 MMR compression, and MMR pages MUST end each coded strip with an EOFB code. Uncompressed data is not allowed.

Profile J is essentially Profile F with JBIG compression (Compression=9) used instead of MH, MR or MMR. JBIG offers improved compression for halftoned originals.
sections.eli5: Profile S is the plainest black-and-white page that everyone can read. F and J are fancier ways to pack the same kind of page into a smaller file.

sections.title: The Color Profiles C, L and M
sections.content:
Profile C is the base profile for color and grayscale fax. It uses lossy baseline JPEG compression (Compression=7) of L*a*b* data, with BitsPerSample=8 and a new PhotometricInterpretation value of 10 (ITULAB) for the encoding defined in ITU-T T.42. All applications that support color fax must support it.

Profile L codes color and grayscale images losslessly with JBIG, following ITU-T T.43. It covers RGB, CMY and CMYK images with one bit per color, palette color images, and continuous-tone color and grayscale images. Profile L files use the color table in the T.43 data stream rather than the TIFF ColorMap field.

Profile M uses Mixed Raster Content (ITU-T T.44), which allows different coding methods and resolutions within one page. It structures a page in three layers: a bi-level Mask and multi-level Foreground and Background layers. Where the Mask pixel is 1 the output pixel comes from the Foreground, and where it is 0 it comes from the Background. In TIFF, the Primary IFD of a page carries one layer and other layers hang off it as child IFDs through the SubIFDs field. A new StripRowCounts field lets strips have a variable number of scanlines, and readers MUST support it.
sections.eli5: For color pages, the page can be split into see-through layers: one for text shapes, one for the text color and one for the photo. Each layer is squashed in the way that suits it best.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says it creates no security issues beyond those already identified in the image/tiff registration (RFC 3302) and in the use of fields defined by TIFF. The new fields it defines are purely descriptive, so no new security risks are incurred.

It adds that the encoding does not preclude using any Internet security protocol to encrypt, authenticate or provide non-repudiation for TIFF-encoded facsimile messages. The MIME content types image/tiff and image/tiff-fx are used for this data, and their registrations are described elsewhere, including in RFC 3950.
sections.eli5: The labels in the file only describe the picture. They do not tell the computer to do anything, so they add no new danger.

sections.title: Changes From RFC 2301
sections.content:
Annex B lists the technical edits made relative to RFC 2301. Among them: FillOrder=1 was added to Profile J; ResolutionUnit was constrained to inch for all color profiles; the ColorMap field was deleted from Profile L because it re-encoded a palette already in the T.43 data stream; and the field DefaultImageColor was renamed ImageBaseColor.

Compression value 9 was redefined to be T.82 (JBIG), with a new T82Options field whose default of 0 corresponds to the T.85 application profile. Several options were dropped for lack of interoperability testing, including 12 bits per sample for JPEG and 13 to 16 bits per sample for palette color.
sections.eli5: After years of real use, the authors fixed some labels, renamed one, and dropped features that nobody had managed to test together.
